s0101.literal: After the breath is cut off, if one simply abandons [the body] in the wild, following the Buddhist dharma of the charnel ground, that is my wish—only I fear it would be too singular.
s0101.idiomatic: After I die, if the body is simply left in the wild per the Buddhist charnel-ground practice, that is my wish—I only fear it would seem too odd.

s0102.literal: Thin boards may be used all around the body, carried on a spirit carriage, covered with reed matting, and buried in a mountain hollow.
s0102.idiomatic: Wrap the body in thin boards, carry it on a funeral cart, cover it with a reed mat, and bury it in a hillside grave.

s0103.literal: Moreover I ultimately have few brothers and no other descendants; Jing is young and does not yet understand affairs—only for three months set out a small couch and incense, fulfilling your brothers' mutual affection, then remove them; do not do useless things.
s0103.idiomatic: I have few brothers and no other heirs; Jing is young and knows nothing of the world. For three months only, set out a small couch and incense to show your brotherly bond, then put them away—do not do anything needless.

s0104.literal: Earlier, when Zhen was in Zhou he once attended the Zhao Prince in study; the prince was the beloved younger brother of Emperor Wu of Zhou and treated him with great courtesy.
s0104.idiomatic: Earlier, while Zhen was in Zhou, he served as reader to the Zhao prince, Emperor Wu of Zhou's beloved younger brother, who treated him with great courtesy.

s0105.literal: The prince once heard attendants say that whenever Zhen was alone he wept day and night; he therefore privately sent to inquire and learned that Zhen's mother was old and far away in the southland, and then said to Zhen: "If I go out to reside in my fief, I shall send the reader home to support [your mother].
s0105.idiomatic: The prince heard from attendants that Zhen wept day and night whenever alone. He sent privately to inquire and learned Zhen's mother was old and far off in the south. He told Zhen, "If I am posted to my fief, I shall send you home to support her.

s0106.literal: " Several years later the prince indeed went out; on taking leave he memorialized face to face, saying: "Xie Zhen is supremely filial and his mother is old; your servant wishes to release him.
s0106.idiomatic: " Years later the prince was indeed posted out. On leave he memorialized in person: "Xie Zhen is deeply filial and his mother is old; I ask that he be released.

s0107.literal: " The emperor marveled at the prince's kindness and released him, and he returned to the state with the envoy Du Zihui.
s0107.idiomatic: " The emperor admired the prince's kindness and let Zhen go; he returned with the envoy Du Zihui.

s0108.literal: His collected writings, because of the military turmoil, for the most part did not survive.
s0108.idiomatic: His collected writings were mostly lost in the wars.

s0110.literal: Sima Hao, styled Wensheng, was a native of Wen in Henei.
s0110.idiomatic: Sima Hao, styled Wensheng, came from Wen in Henei.

s0111.literal: His founding ancestor Rouzhi was Jin Palace Attendant and Director of the Imperial Secretariat; as grandson of the Prince of Nandun he continued the line of Prince Xian of Qi, Wang You.
s0111.idiomatic: His founding ancestor Rouzhi had been Jin palace attendant and director of the imperial secretariat; as grandson of the Prince of Nandun he descended from Prince Xian of Qi, Wang You.

s0112.literal: His father Zichan was Liang Minister of the Masters of Writing for the Water Bureau and Administrator of Yueyang—namely, the maternal elder brother of Emperor Wu of Liang.
s0112.idiomatic: His father Zichan had been Liang minister of the masters of writing for the water bureau and administrator of Yueyang—the maternal elder brother of Emperor Wu of Liang.

s0113.literal: Hao from youth was clever and alert, with utmost nature.
s0113.idiomatic: Hao was clever and alert from youth, with a deeply filial nature.

s0114.literal: At age twelve he suffered inner mourning; childlike devotion exceeded the rites, and for nearly ten days he took no water or gruel.
s0114.idiomatic: At twelve he mourned his mother; his grief exceeded the rites, and for nearly ten days he took no food or drink.

s0115.literal: Whenever he wailed in grief he would fall into stupefaction; kin inside and outside all feared he could not endure the mourning.
s0115.idiomatic: Each time he wailed he would faint; kin far and near feared he could not survive the mourning.

s0116.literal: Father Zichan repeatedly exhorted him and forced him to take gruel, yet he was wasted to the bone.
s0116.idiomatic: His father Zichan urged him repeatedly and forced gruel on him, yet he was wasted to the bone.

s0117.literal: When mourning ended, as a kinsman by marriage and a younger clansman he was admitted to audience; Emperor Wu of Liang saw Hao emaciated, sighed a long while, and said to father and son Zichan:
s0117.idiomatic: When mourning ended he entered audience as a kinsman by marriage. Emperor Wu of Liang saw how thin Hao was, sighed long, and said to Zichan:

s0118.literal: "Yesterday I saw Luo'er's face haggard—it moves one to pity; he does not fall short of the family tradition—he is a son indeed.
s0118.idiomatic: "Yesterday I saw Luo'er's haggard face and pitied him; he does not betray the family tradition—here is a true son.

s0120.literal: On first appointment he was Erudite of the Imperial Academy and was repeatedly promoted to Regular Attendant.
s0120.idiomatic: He began as erudite of the imperial academy and rose to regular attendant.

s0121.literal: On father's mourning his grief-destruction was still more severe; he built a hut beside the tomb, and within a single day took only one sheng of thin wheat gruel.
s0121.idiomatic: When his father died his mourning was still more severe; he built a hut by the tomb and ate only one sheng of thin wheat gruel a day.

s0122.literal: The tomb was at Xinlin, adjoining mountain heights where formerly there were many fierce beasts; Hao built his hut for several years and wolves and jackals vanished.
s0122.idiomatic: The tomb was at Xinlin among hills once full of beasts; Hao kept his hut for years and wolves and jackals vanished.

s0123.literal: Two turtledoves always roosted at the hut, tame beyond the ordinary; in Xinlin the tale is still told.
s0123.idiomatic: Two doves always roosted at the hut, unusually tame; Xinlin still tells of it.

s0124.literal: In the Chengsheng era he was made Junior Tutor to the Heir Apparent.
s0124.idiomatic: In the Chengsheng era he was made junior tutor to the heir apparent.

s0125.literal: When Jiangling fell he followed the usual course into the Pass; the Liang house slaughtered the crown prince and burial was lost, and Hao as a palace officer therefore submitted a bold memorial to the Zhou court requesting return to Jiangling for reburial—the wording was very bitter.
s0125.idiomatic: When Jiangling fell he went to the north as others did. The Liang house had slaughtered the crown prince and left the burial lost; as a palace officer Hao submitted a bold memorial to Zhou to return and rebury him, in words very bitter.

s0126.literal: The Zhou court replied with a gracious edict, saying: "In old times when Zhufu Yan followed execution, Kong Che had an elder's bearing; when Peng Yue met execution, Luan Bu received a subject's rites.
s0126.idiomatic: Zhou replied graciously: "When Zhufu Yan was executed, Kong Che showed an elder's bearing; when Peng Yue was put to death, Luan Bu received a subject's rites.

s0127.literal: Though the Junior Tutor's native state has changed, he still cherishes the feeling of seeing one off on the journey—only thus is loyalty tested and the way of the subject known; let Jingzhou at once bury him with rites."
s0127.idiomatic: Though the junior tutor's country has changed, he still feels the duty of escorting the dead—thus loyalty and subjecthood are proved; let Jingzhou bury him with full rites."

s0128.literal: In the eighth year of Taijian, returning from Zhou to court, Emperor Xuan especially granted him special honors and increased rewards.
s0128.idiomatic: In Taijian year 8, returning from Zhou, Emperor Xuan granted him special honors and rich rewards.

s0129.literal: He was made Staff Adviser to the Prince of Yidu, moved to Director of the Long Autumn Office of the Andre Palace, Direct and Upright Attendant of the Scattered Cavalry, Grand Master of the Palace, and Senior Rectifier of Sizhou, and died in office.
s0129.idiomatic: He was made staff adviser to the Prince of Yidu, then director of the long autumn office of the Andre palace, direct and upright attendant of the scattered cavalry, grand master of the palace, and senior rectifier of Sizhou, and died in office.

s0130.literal: He had a collection in ten fascicles.
s0130.idiomatic: He left a collection in ten fascicles.

s0131.literal: His son Yanyi, styled Xizhong, from youth was deep and keen, fond of learning.
s0131.idiomatic: His son Yanyi, styled Xizhong, was from youth deep-minded, keen, and fond of learning.

s0132.literal: When Jiangling fell he followed his father into the Pass.
s0132.idiomatic: When Jiangling fell he followed his father into the north.

s0133.literal: On mother's mourning his observance exceeded the rites.
s0133.idiomatic: When his mother died his mourning exceeded the rites.

s0134.literal: When Hao returned to the capital, Yanyi personally shouldered the bier, traveling by day hidden and by night on the road, braving frost and ice until hands and feet were all chapped with cold sores.
s0134.idiomatic: When Hao returned to the capital, Yanyi shouldered the bier himself, hiding by day and traveling by night through frost and ice until his hands and feet were chapped with cold sores.

s0135.literal: On reaching the capital, because of wind-cold in the middle he then suffered contracture and paralysis and was several years before he recovered.
s0135.idiomatic: At the capital he took a chill that left him paralyzed for years before he recovered.

s0136.literal: He was gradually promoted to Recorder of the Prince of Poyang, Friend of the Prince of Yuanling, and Attendant of the Masters of Writing under the Minister of Works.
s0136.idiomatic: He rose to recorder of the Prince of Poyang, friend of the Prince of Yuanling, and attendant of the masters of writing under the minister of works.

s0137.literal: Zhang Zhao, styled Deming, was a native of Wu in Wu commandery.
s0137.idiomatic: Zhang Zhao, styled Deming, came from Wu in Wu commandery.

s0138.literal: From youth he had a filial nature; in tending his parents' countenance he was very careful, and in ritual there was nothing contrary.
s0138.idiomatic: From youth he was filial; he tended his parents' mood with great care and never breached ritual.

s0139.literal: His father Yan often suffered from wasting thirst and craved fresh fish; Zhao himself netted fish to supply morning and evening.
s0139.idiomatic: His father Yan suffered wasting thirst and craved fresh fish; Zhao netted fish himself for every meal.

s0140.literal: His younger brother Gan, styled Xuanming, was clever, keen, and broadly learned, and also had utmost nature.
s0140.idiomatic: His younger brother Gan, styled Xuanming, was clever, learned, and deeply filial.

s0141.literal: When their father died the brothers both wore no silk or brocade and ate no salt or vinegar, each day taking only one sheng of wheat-bran gruel.
s0141.idiomatic: When their father died the brothers wore no silk and ate no salt or vinegar, living on one sheng of wheat-bran gruel a day.

s0142.literal: Whenever grief moved them they would vomit blood; neighbors hearing their weeping all wept for them.
s0142.idiomatic: Each surge of grief made them vomit blood; neighbors wept when they heard them cry.

s0143.literal: Before father's mourning had ended, mother née Lu also died; the brothers then mourned in destruction for six years, their forms wasted to the bone, and kin and friends who saw them did not recognize them.
s0143.idiomatic: Before their father's mourning ended their mother, née Lu, died too; for six years the brothers mourned until they were wasted to the bone, and friends who saw them did not know them.

s0144.literal: The family was poor and could not afford a full burial; they therefore wore plain cloth and ate vegetables for more than ten years, shut their door and did not go out, and cut off human affairs.
s0144.idiomatic: Too poor for a full burial, they wore plain cloth and ate vegetables for more than ten years, shut their door, and cut off the world.

s0145.literal: At that time the Prince of Hengyang, Bo Xin, was administering the commandery and recommended Gan as Filial and Incorrupt; he firmly declined and did not accept.
s0145.idiomatic: When the Prince of Hengyang, Bo Xin, governed the commandery he recommended Gan as filial and incorrupt; Gan firmly declined.

s0146.literal: The brothers both fell ill through mourning-destruction; Zhao lost one eye and Gan also suffered from cold affliction and chronic illness; both died at home before fifty, and sons and heirs were cut off.
s0146.idiomatic: Both brothers fell ill from excessive mourning; Zhao lost an eye and Gan suffered chronic chills; both died at home before fifty, and left no heirs.

s0147.literal: In Emperor Xuan's time there was one Wang Zhixuan of Taiyuan, sojourning in Yan county of Kuaiji commandery; at home he was famed for filial piety.
s0147.idiomatic: In Emperor Xuan's time Wang Zhixuan of Taiyuan lived as a sojourner in Yan county, Kuaiji, and was famed at home for filial piety.

s0148.literal: When he suffered father's mourning he died from grief-destruction; Emperor Xuan commended this and ordered that the lane where he lived, Qingku Lane, be changed to "Filial Home Lane."
s0148.idiomatic: When his father died he mourned himself to death; Emperor Xuan praised him and renamed his lane, Qingku, "Filial Home Lane."

s0149.literal: The historiographer says: Among human relations no virtue is greater than filial piety; therefore returning to the root and source, exhausting nature and probing spirit—"Filial, only filial"—it cannot but be urged.
s0149.idiomatic: The historiographer says: Among human bonds no virtue exceeds filial piety; to return to one's origins, exhaust one's nature, and probe the spirit—"Filial, only filial"—cannot but be urged.

s0150.literal: Thus the Record says "it fills Heaven and Earth"—how grand!
s0150.idiomatic: The Record says it "fills Heaven and Earth"—how grand!

s0152.literal: Zu Sui: the character "sui" in the Book of Liang and the Southern History biography of Xie Lin both read "jing."
s0152.idiomatic: On "Zu Sui": the character sui in the Book of Liang and the Southern History biography of Xie Lin both read jing.

s0153.literal: Houzhu thereupon charged palace attendant Shi Wenqing, saying: the character "qing" in the base text was wrongly written "you"; other editions are not in error; now corrected.
s0153.idiomatic: On "Houzhu thereupon charged palace attendant Shi Wenqing": the base text wrongly wrote you for qing in Wenqing; other editions are correct; now emended.
